messages.subject: GLM & Instrumental Variables in stan?
parts: Does anyone have any suggestions/examples for coding the estimation of instrumental variables in stan using GLM? The only example I could find uses a multivariate normal likelihood. I basically want to do the two stages using a logit model. Can I just use a multivariate normal model and then use a logit link on that output or is there a better way to do this in stan?

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: GLM & Instrumental Variables in stan?
parts:
On Thursday, August 6, 2015 at 8:03:53 AM UTC-4, Richard McAlexander wrote:
Does anyone have any suggestions/examples for coding the estimation of instrumental variables in stan using GLM? The only example I could find uses a multivariate normal likelihood. I basically want to do the two stages using a logit model. Can I just use a multivariate normal model and then use a logit link on that output or is there a better way to do this in stan?

Use a bivariate normal likelihood (composed of a univariate normal distribution for the outcome times a conditional normal distribution for the instrumented variable) is much easier because the dependence is characterized by a correlation, which is easily understood and something one could specify a prior on. In the bivariate distributions where one margin is normal and the other is logistic, the dependence could be captured by any copula but is harder to interpret. Many ignore the fact that the instrumented variable is binary when the CACE they want to estimate is additive but it is usually better to estimate a Tobin-5 model with a bivariate normal distribution for latent utility and the outcome, whose log-likelihood is given in the vignette for the sampleSelection R package.

Ben

parts:
On Friday, August 7, 2015 at 12:02:52 PM UTC-4, Richard McAlexander wrote:
first equation: instrument ~ thing that predicts instrument
second equation: outcome of interest ~ thing I'm trying to instrument for + controls
third equation: outcome of interest ~ other possible predictor + controls

It is more like

first equation: T ~ controls + things that predict treatment but not outcomes conditional on the controls
second equation: (Y | T = 1) ~ controls
third equation: (Y | T = 0) ~ controls

with a 3x3 covariance matrix among the errors with the first variance restricted to 1.

The Tobin-5 model allows the intercept and coefficients to differ depending on whether T = 1 or T = 0. The LATE can be computed by averaging differences in the posterior predictive distribution where you counterfactually use the parameters from the second equation for the observations where T = 0 and use the parameters from the third equation for the observations where T = 1 (in addition to the factual posterior predictive distributions where you use the parameters from the second equation for the observations where T = 1 and use the parameters from the third equation for the observations where T = 0).

Ben

On Sunday, August 9, 2015 at 12:24:26 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I'll have to flag this more heavily in the manual, but you almost
always want to use Cholesky factors rather than full matrices as
data types.

There's an error in the manual example for multivariate priors in
that you need to pre-multiply, not post-multiply.

Luc's suggestion to use quad_form_diag() was a good one, although it is not really noticeable with 3x3 matrices.

This is actually one of the rare cases where it makes sense to use a 3x3 correlation matrix rather than a Cholesky factor of a 3x3 correlation matrix. Part of the reason is that the likelihood is written in terms of scalars, so you don't get the benefit of using multi_normal_cholesky() rather than multi_normal(). But the main reason --- which is the most fascinating thing about this model from a Bayesian perspective and makes frequentists' heads asplode --- is that the [3,2] correlation does not enter the likelihood but your prior beliefs about it have a major affect on the posterior distribution of the [1,2] correlation, the [1,3] correlation, and of every other parameter.

The [3,2] correlation is the correlation between the errors for Y | T = 1 and Y | T = 0, and because no one is in both the treatment and the control group at the same time, the likelihood doesn't identify the [3,2] correlation. So, if you do MLE or a two-step estimator, you don't even optimize over the [3,2] correlation. But if you are a genuine Bayesian, then you have beliefs about the [3,2] correlation and in most situations, those beliefs are that the [3,2] correlation is really close to 1.0 (i.e. whatever is omitted from the model of the outcome when T = 1 presumably has an essentially equal effect when T = 0). Moreover, if the  [3,2] correlation is really close to 1.0, then there are relatively few values  of the [1,2] correlation (between the error in the model for T and the error in the model for Y | T = 1) and the [1,3] correlation (between the error in the model for T and the error in the model for Y | T = 0) that satisfy the positive definiteness constraint on the 3x3 correlation matrix as a whole. 

So, for a Tobin-5 model I like to "omit" the prior on Lambda (implicitly putting a joint uniform prior over the space of 3x3 correlation matrices) and overlay a beta prior on (1 + Lambda[3,2]) / 2 (ignoring the Jacobian warning from the parser because this transformation only involves constants). If first shape parameter is much larger than the second shape parameter in this beta prior, that implies Lambda[3,2] is close to 1.0 and consequently affects the distribution of Lambda[1,2] and Lambda[1,3].

Ben

parts: This
> covmat <- diag_pre_multiply(sdvector, diag_post_multiply(Lambda, sdvector));

should be

covmat <- quad_form_diag(Lambda, sdvector);

Same result, but more efficient.

I'd also suggest moving the definition of "constant" to a
transformed data block so the user can't mess it up. And coming
up with a more descriptive name.

It's also good to come up with consistent naming, so that these
would all match:

> real beta_treat;
> real betaselect;
> real beta_untreat;

It'll save you time in the long run and make the programs easier to
read (I'd recommend the underscore version).

I'd also suggest more spaces, and when you have repeated subexpressions,
as in
> lp[i]<-constant+(-log(sigma2)-0.5*((y_ss[i]-beta_treat*x_ss[i])/sigma2)^2+log(Phi((betaselect*xselect[i]+(ratio_treat)*(y_ss[i]-beta_treat*x_ss[i]))/((1-Lambda[1,3]^2)^.5))));

defining something like

beta_treat_x_ss_i <- beta_treat * x_ss[i]
